Diabulimia nearly killed me

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Diabulimia is an eating disorder where Type 1 diabetes patients deliberately give themselves less insulin in order to lose weight

Kyla was diagnosed with Type 1 Diabetes when she was 16. At the time she already suffered from Bulimia and anorexia. She was as thin as could be and worked hard at keeping it that way. After being diagnosed with type 1 diabetes she started taking her prescribed dose of insulin and she started to put on weight. She soon figured out that If she withheld the insulin, her weight would come down. So her life spiralled into a very abusive relationship between her body and her mind. The side effects of withholding her insulin put her in hospital more times than she can count, she lost the vision in her right eye, had two toes amputated, but still she refused to take the insulin. She was diagnosed with Diabulimia, but refused to get help. Until this eating disorder threatened her ability to walk. She landed up in hospital and the doctors feared for days that Kyla’s foot would have to amputated. After she walked out of the hospital that week she agreed to being admitted for the treatment of her Diabulimia.

Today Kyla is still battling and has to go to meetings every week to keep herself healthy. She has lost her job and her long term partner. From 16 – 32 years old she destroyed everything around her, because she was addicted to being thin.


Further information:
Kyla describes what it is like to decide to withhold the medication she needs to survive in order to stay thin.
Visuals: the insulin injection, the dosage, her weighing herself

Voice over: Diabulimia is an eating disorder where Type 1 diabetes patients deliberatly withhold their prescribed insulin intake in order to lose weight

Kyla starts telling her story:
I was diagnosed with Diabtetes when I was 16 years old. At that point I was Already Anorexic and bulimic.
She talks about why she had these pre-existing eating disorders and the family dynamic that she feels made her want to control her food intake.

Scene: Kyla and her mom are eating a meal together (possibly with the presenter) and her mom explains how every time the phone rang she thought it was someone to tell her Kyla was dead.

Specialts: An endocrinoligist speaks about when Diabulimia was first discovered and why it has not been registered as an official mental health problem. What the prevelance is in South Africa? Is it being underdiagnosed? Treatment for it?
Signs to look out for?

Kyla talks about the turning point that got her to go for therapy.
Kyla goes to a group session or some type of therapy for the diabulimia at Imani clinic
Speak to the specialists about how to treat this eating disorder.

Kyla: talks about healing. How she weighs herself less, tries to take her insulin as prescribed and eat enough for a body mass index. She is trying to learn to love herself again.
She wants to help other girls not go through the hell she has been through.
Visual: Kyla doing something that is part of her journey to learning to love herself.

Press Release:


Diabulimia Eating Disorder
Withholding medication vital to one’s survival in order to stay skinny: it’s called Diabulimia. This eating disorder sees Type 1 diabetics deliberately giving themselves less insulin in order to lose weight. Carte Blanche hears from brave people battling their addiction to being thin and paying the tragic cost of their destructive choice, from blindness to loss of limbs and more.


Script:


Time code CHARACTER / VISUAL
1 00:00 Jade in her house explaining when she got diagnosed Jade: I was first diagnosed in 1994, I was 8 years old I remember it was the day of the elections, the 1994 elections that I got really sick and fell into a coma. I woke up and they just said you are diabetic and you know your life is probably going to change.

2 00:21 Kate introduction and when she was diagnosed. Montage of her taking her insulin Kate: I had a really bad car accident when I was 14 and one of the reasons that it can develop is an auto immune response so your body attacks the pancreas and kills the cells that make insulin.
3 00:36 Jade with her insulin Jade: I felt like my diabetes was directly associated to like my weight, because my weight used to fluctuate a lot. I just felt like fat all the time
4 00:47 Kate interview Kate: when I was diagnosed I was pretty thin, and then as soon as you start using insulin obviously your body starts behaving normally again and I didn’t go over weight but I picked up really fast because of that and it was alarming and I just stopped injecting.
5 01:00 Claire Mawisa speaks to camera. Link. Claire: Kate, not her real name and Jade both suffer from Diabulimia – an eating disorder where type 1 diabetics deliberately limit their insulin intake to lose weight. Globally 30% of female type 1 diabetics suffer from an eating disorder
6 01:19 The Centre for Diabetes sign with interview of Dr. Larry Larry: People with type 1 diabetes their lives revolve much around food they’ve got to understand the carbohydrate content of their food, balance carbohydrate insulin dosage so food becomes central to their lifestyle and therefore it becomes their target in women who or girls who have a psychological issue
7 01:47 Jade speaks to Claire


Jade: Diabetes almost is like a nuisance as a young person you would forget to take your insulin that would like an innocent forgetting then slowly I started to realize that I’m actually getting skinny now and I can eat whatever I want to and still it just stays off. I’d feel like crap but you get all these compliments from people “ oh you loosing so much weight and you look good” or it kind of like takes over. If I knew I was going out or had to be in a costume or something like that that’s when I’d obviously not take the insulin because I didn’t want to look fat in my bikini. Like it was both the problem and the solution at the same time.
8 02:32 Kate on her bed,
Cut to interview to camera Kate: You are incredibly nauseous all the time, everything heals very very slowly you are incredibly thirsty and completely feel off kilter you are exhausted all the time and it gets really really bad theres so much in your blood that you caint breath properly like huffing and puffing sounds like I had to be on oxygen
9 02:52 Dr Larry Larry: I think that diabulimia is part of a spectrum at the most be known side they might miss the odd injection to miss a meal that goes right through to the full blown anorexia and diabulimia fits toward the end of the spectrum where they tend to over eat then vomit to keep their weight down so that they don’t take the insulin. So rather than taking insulin and food and the two balance what you do is you don’t take insulin and you don’t take food, but you don’t want to be seen not to eat so you eat in public then go vomit and they know intellectually what they are doing and understand the effects of it but the obsession with weight overrides that
10 03:36 Kate montage as she weighs herself Kate: I was doing all this damage to my myself and I knew all of the consequinces that were coming, the damage to my organs and I couldn’t stop. That becomes your entire definition that is who you are atleast you ar that, atleast im thinner than that person
11 04:00 Jade interview with Claire Jade: you are constantly reminded about the complications of diabetes or you know the side effects of bad sugar control but I think it kind of takes a second seat to actually feeling like confident
12 04:18 Kate interview Kate: I was constantly trying to not inject enough to, to keep not injecting but I have to inject myself to keep myself. I was still in the danger zone but to keep myself out of hospital. I have definitely been to hospitals over 15 times for that. When I say I went into hospital I went into ICU

Claire: What are the long term side effects been?

Kate: I think for me? Physically so what’s happening now, I can’t see properly from my right eye ball its really really blurry there is a lot of physical damage. It damages the nerves in my heart, there’s a dead nerve in my leg so I can’t walk as I used to. I have had two toes amputated its hugely shameful.

Claire: Besides your physical toll, what about your friendships and relationship and your lifestyle.

Kate: It’s been so much time locked away at home, not doing things because I was too out of my mind or to like needing to purge to do it. I miss a lot of things, I missed a lot of celebrations and time with people I just miss a lot of time

13 05:41 Dr Larry speaking about the side effects Larry: Its not a medical condition is a psychological condition. These patients must be seen by a trained psychiatrist, like any eating disorder. The psychiatrist trained in anorexia, bulimia and don’t worry about the diabetes you will sort out the primary psychological problem. I can diagnose it but until the mental side is sorted out we can’t do anything about it as physicians.

14 06:04 Google search of the term Diabulimia Jade: I had come across articles on the internet and done a bit of research to see if there were other people doing the same thing. That’s when I came across the term diabulimia. It made it seem so much more real, so much more wrong and almost like am I killing myself now?

15 06:27 Dr Larry speaks to Claire Mawisa Larry: With the eating disorder like diabulimia and anorexia the thyroid can be as low as 5% and those that little survive often survive with severe long-term complications like blindness and kidney failure they don’t do well. This being said anorexia or bulimia and diabetes together are a death sentence
16 06:51 Kate talks to cameras Kate: The way I eventually ended up going to treatment is that I developed a big ulcer, you could see there was black on my foot there was dead cells. There was 80% chance they were going to amputate my foot. And eventually my best friend, her mom is my other mom she was like “this is ridiculous people will stop talking to you need to go to rehab” I intended on staying for 2 weeks I ended up staying for four months.
17 07:20 Voice over with montage of Kate measuring herself V/O: After over 10 years of battling with diabulimia, both Jade and Kate may have lost their teenage years but they are in recovery and determined to live
18 07:30 Jade speaks to camera. Intercut with her in the kitchen with her husband Jade: there’s bigger things than my weight, there’s future plans and wanting to have a child and conseve my own child not having to think about other options that are a bit more important and force me to do better
19 08:00 Kate ending Kate: there’s been a feeling for, even in recovery for a long long time of waiting to start my life and now I just want to have my life, I am I think everyday. I feel a lot more open to things whatever comes and to be present and respond to things
